'''Roger Paman''' (c. 1700 - 1748) was an 18th-century English [[mathematician]].

== Life and work ==
Very little is known about the life of Roger Paman. He cited a professor of [[St John's College, Cambridge]] as mentor, so it is possible that he studied at [[Cambridge University]].<ref name=Smestad51>{{smallcaps|Smestad}} Chapter 5.1</ref>

As he explains in the preface of his only published book, he participated in [[George Anson's voyage around the world]] (1740–1744), but he returned to England in 1742 with one of two ships which returned before the end of the expedition.<ref>{{smallcaps|Appleby}}, page 200.</ref> Before embarking on the expedition, he left his mathematical papers to philosopher [[David Hartley (philosopher)|David Hartley]].<ref>{{smallcaps|Jesseph}}, page 285.</ref>

His papers were presented to the [[Royal Society]] in 1742 and, as a result, he was named ''fellow'' of the institution in 1743.<ref name="Smestad51" />

In 1745 his book "The Harmony of the Ancient and Modern Geometry Asserted" was published in London. The book is a reply to the mathematical concepts of [[George Berkeley]] in his book ''[[The Analyst]]'' (1734).<ref>{{smallcaps|Breidert}}, pages 119–123.</ref> The originality of this book lies in the development of all the calculus in finite differences, in order to avoid the paradoxes of infinity explained by Berkeley.<ref>{{smallcaps|Jesseph}}, page 287.</ref> Paman presents in his book the concepts of ''minimaius'' and ''maximinus'', a far antecedent of the mathematical concepts of [[infimum and supremum]].<ref>{{smallcaps|Smestad}}, chapter 5.3.1</ref><ref>{{smallcaps|Jesseph}}, pages 287–290.</ref>
